opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just economics and incentives. If you look at where the energy goes right now, most people take an open model, the weights, and treat it as a black box. They fine-tune it, they put a RAG pipeline around it, they build an agent on top. That's where you can ship something in a week and show a demo. Actually going inside the model, changing the attention mechanism, the architecture, how the layers interact, that requires a very different skill set and, frankly, a lot of compute to validate. Any architectural change, if you want to know whether it really works, you have to train at a scale where the results mean something. That's out of reach for most academic labs and most startups.

There's also a path-dependency thing. When we wrote the transformer paper, the idea was partly that it was simple and parallelizable, and that made it easy to scale. Then everyone converged on it, and now the whole stack is optimized around it: the kernels, the hardware, the inference servers, the training recipes. So if you come up with something that's maybe theoretically better, you're fighting the whole ecosystem. Your idea runs slower on today's GPUs because nobody wrote the optimized kernels for it, and it looks worse just because of that.

And the third piece is that "open" often means open weights, not open process. You get the final artifact but not the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints, the ablations that tell you why things are the way they are. Without that, experimenting with the internals is like reverse-engineering. You can do interpretability work, which is great and is growing, but really modifying and retraining is hard when you don't know what went into it.

So I think if we want more innovation at that level, we need more truly open development, where data, code, and checkpoints are shared, and some way to pool compute so researchers can actually test ideas at meaningful scale. That's something I care about a lot. I think it's important for AI not to be controlled by just a few companies, and making the internals accessible is a big part of that.

r001.rationale: The response attributes limited experimentation to incentives, skill and compute costs, ecosystem lock-in, and incomplete openness. It does not say that people invest less because they view open models as inferior to closed models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly I think it comes down to a couple of things that are more sociological than technical.

The first is just incentives. When a lab releases open weights, what they're really releasing is an artifact, not a research program. The paper, if there is one, describes the recipe at a high level, but the actual decisions — why this attention variant, why this data mix, why this learning rate schedule — are buried in internal experiments that never get published. So the people outside who pick it up are mostly treating it as a black box they can fine-tune or run inference on. That's where the immediate value is. If you're a startup, you're not going to get paid for discovering that layer 17 does something interesting. You get paid for shipping a product on top of it.

The second thing is cost. Even with open weights, really experimenting with the internals — ablating components, retraining with changes, doing proper mechanistic work — requires compute that most academic groups and individuals just don't have. You can poke at activations on a single GPU, and there's great interpretability work happening there, but if you want to ask "what happens if we change this architectural choice and train from scratch," you're back to needing a cluster. So the experimentation that does happen tends to be the cheap kind: prompting, LoRA, quantization. Those are useful, but they're not really touching the internals.

And the third is that the field has sort of converged. Everyone is training roughly the same transformer with roughly the same tweaks, and there's a strong prior now that scale matters more than architecture. So the perceived expected value of fiddling with internals has gone down. People assume the big labs have already tried the obvious things, and if those worked, they'd be in the model already. I actually think that assumption is wrong in a lot of cases — the big labs are optimizing for a very specific objective on a very specific budget, and there's a lot of design space they just haven't explored because it doesn't fit their roadmap.

What I'd love to see is more infrastructure that makes the internals legible and cheap to modify. Open weights without open training code, open data, and open eval harnesses is only half open. Once you have the full pipeline reproducible at small scale, you lower the barrier for someone to say, "Okay, let me actually try swapping this piece out and see what happens." That's where you get the kind of distributed experimentation that made the early deep learning years so productive — lots of people trying weird things, most of which fail, but a few of which turn into the next big idea.

r001.rationale: The response cites incentives, compute costs, and assumptions that major labs have already tried obvious changes. It does not attribute lower investment to a belief that open models are inferior to closed models.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that having access to the weights is only one piece of what you need. If you want to change something fundamental inside the model, you need a way to train it, the data to train it on, and enough compute to tell whether your idea actually works. So the model can be open, but the ability to experiment with it is still pretty expensive.

And then there’s the feedback loop. If you’re experimenting with prompts or fine-tuning, you can get a useful result relatively quickly. If you change the architecture, a bad result is harder to interpret. Is the idea wrong, or does it need different training settings, or more training? That makes it a much bigger research commitment.

So I think you naturally see more effort going into using the models. Making experimentation with the internals cheaper and easier to reproduce would help more people explore that space.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains limited experimentation through training costs, compute, data, and slower feedback. It does not say that people invest less because they view open models as inferior to closed models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that open weights are only one piece of what you need to experiment. You can download a model and run it, but understanding why it behaves a certain way—and then changing that behavior—requires a lot more context. What data was it trained on? What experiments led to this architecture? What happens if you change one component and retrain it?

And the feedback loop is expensive. If you build an application on top of a model, you can try something and see the result pretty quickly. If you change the internals, you may need substantial compute just to find out whether your idea works. So naturally, more people work at the application layer.

I think there's also an accessibility issue. We need better tools for inspecting models and running controlled experiments, so that you don't have to reproduce an entire training effort to test one hypothesis. Open weights make that possible in principle, but there's still work to do to make it practical for more people.

r001.rationale: The response points to missing training context, costly experimentation, and limited tooling as reasons for less work on model internals. It does not say open models are viewed as inferior to closed models.
